item.title: Subsidised fertiliser being smuggled into Myanmar
item.description:
Aman paddy has been cultivated on nearly 500 acres of land in Uttar Pukuria village of Rajapalong Union in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar. More than a hundred farmers in the village have complained that they are unable to obtain urea fertiliser, which they need after transplanting the rice seedlings.

Mohammad Tayyub, 45, a resident of the village, is one of these farmers. He said he went to a dealer in Ukhiya Bazar on 30 September to buy 30kg of fertiliser. After waiting in line for nearly seven hours, he received only 5kg. He is worried about how he will protect the crops on his seven kani of land (one kani equals 40 decimals) with this amount of fertiliser.

Like Tayyub, other farmers in the village are also worried about the fertiliser shortage. It has been learned after speaking to farmers that the shortage is not limited to Ukhiya; most areas of Cox’s Bazar, including Teknaf, Ramu, Eidgaon, Pekua and Chakaria, are also facing a fertiliser crisis. The crisis is worsening day by day as several syndicates smuggle fertiliser into Myanmar.

Smuggling into Myanmar

Speaking to officials of the Department of Agricultural Extension and fertiliser dealers, it was learnt that the government provides substantial subsidies on fertiliser sales to ensure that farmers receive fertiliser at affordable prices. Currently, the government-fixed price of a 50kg sack of urea fertiliser at the open market or dealer level is Tk 1,350 (Tk 27 per kg).

However, a sack of fertiliser sells for more than Tk 8,000 in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. As a result, several syndicates are smuggling fertiliser allocated to farmers into Myanmar in pursuit of higher profits. In exchange, consignments of drugs are brought into the country.

A research report recently published by the World Bank stated that nearly 80 per cent of the Agriculture Ministry's budget is spent on fertiliser subsidies. These subsidies have helped maintain agricultural production and price stability.

Speaking to traders involved in imports and exports through Teknaf Land Port, it was learnt that urea fertiliser and fuel oil are being smuggled from Bangladesh into Rakhine State by taking advantage of geographical proximity and the unstable internal situation in Myanmar. Smuggling syndicates involved in the trade bring yaba and crystal meth from Myanmar in exchange for fertiliser and fuel oil.

There is no urea fertiliser manufacturing plant in Rakhine State. Moreover, the unstable situation has disrupted the supply of fertiliser to the state, prompting local farmers to buy fertiliser smuggled from Bangladesh at higher prices.

According to information from the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and the Coast Guard, between 1 June and 20 September this year, the BGB and Coast Guard seized 247,908kg of urea fertiliser in separate drives along the Teknaf, Ukhiya and Naikhongchhari borders and the Naf River. During this period, 127 people involved in smuggling were arrested.

Most recently, on 2 October, the BGB seized 81 sacks of urea fertiliser and smuggled goods worth Tk 700,000 during a drive along the Ghumdhum border in Naikhongchhari.

Lieutenant Colonel Md Foyezul Kabir, commanding officer of the Naikhongchhari 11 BGB, said surveillance along the border had been strengthened to prevent smuggling of fertiliser, fuel oil and other goods.

Locals said fertiliser and fuel oil were being smuggled through at least 23 border points, including Anjumanpara and Balukhali in Palongkhali, Ukhiya; Whykong, Kanjarpara and Ulubunia in Teknaf; Leda and Damdamiya in Hnila; and Ghumdhum in Naikhongchhari. In most cases, the people assisting in the smuggling are arrested, but the masterminds remain beyond the reach of law enforcement agencies.

Coast Guard media officer Lieutenant Commander Sabbir Alam said more than 70 smugglers had already been arrested, along with fertiliser-laden trawlers, during Coast Guard operations while they were attempting to smuggle fertiliser into Myanmar through coastal waters. Efforts were underway to bring the masterminds to justice as well.

M Gafur Uddin Chowdhury, chairman of Palongkhali Union Parishad in Ukhiya, said those involved in smuggling fertiliser and fuel were also bringing in consignments of yaba, ice and other drugs. There are no legitimate transactions in dollars or taka on the other side of the border (Myanmar), he added.

Shahjahan Chowdhury, a member of parliament from Cox’s Bazar-4 (Ukhiya-Teknaf) constituency, said several syndicates were involved in fertiliser smuggling. Although law enforcement agencies had seized large quantities of fertiliser and major consignments of yaba and arrested smugglers during raids, the masterminds remained beyond their reach. They must be identified and brought to justice, he said.

Farmers in distress

Gias Uddin, a farmer from Whykong Union in Teknaf, said, “I am going from one dealer to another in search of fertiliser, but I am not getting the amount I need. Yet fertiliser is being smuggled across the border almost every day.”

Abdul Gafur, a farmer from Kochubunia in Teknaf Sadar Union, said those with smaller plots of land somehow manage to get fertiliser, but farmers with larger plots are unable to obtain the amount they need. Dealers are selling fertiliser to many people who are not farmers. Later, these fertiliser stocks are handed over to smuggling syndicates.

Nawab Mia, a farmer from the Kachhapia area of Ramu, said he cultivated paddy on seven kani of land, but dealers turned him away, saying there was ‘no fertiliser available’. Left with no choice, he bought a small quantity of fertiliser from the market at double the price and spread it across his fields. Due to the continued shortage, Aman seedlings on one and a half kani of his land have turned yellow and are at risk of being destroyed.

Mohammad Kabir, president of the Ukhiya Upazila Fertiliser Dealers Association, said some unscrupulous traders were smuggling fertiliser allocated to farmers into Myanmar to make extra profits. As a result, fertiliser was not available in Ukhiya according to demand.

Regarding fertiliser smuggling, Bimal Kumar Pramanik, deputy director of the Department of Agricultural Extension, said several teams were monitoring markets to prevent smuggling. Special attention was being given to fertiliser sales in Teknaf and Ukhiya upazilas.

Dealers were submitting information on fertiliser sales to the Department of Agricultural Extension online after completing sales. Even so, action would be taken against the dealers concerned if allegations of illegal fertiliser sales were found to be true, he added.

item.title: 45th BCS: Recommended but dropped, allegations of state injustice; state minister assures re-verification
item.description:
Aleya Khanam is a self-respecting and hardworking woman from West Bejgram village in Hatibandha upazila of Lalmonirhat. Through her hard-earned income, she has raised her three children to be educated and responsible citizens. Her eldest daughter has completed her studies and settled down, while her youngest daughter has just started college. Her son, Shamim Al Mahadi, completed his studies at Bangladesh Agricultural University and was preparing for the Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examination.

Alongside farming, Aleya Khanam built her own cattle farm at home in an effort to become financially self-reliant. A year ago, when she received the news that her son had been finally recommended for appointment through the 45th BCS examination, she felt proud of him. She thought his merit had received its due recognition.

But that relief did not last long. Eleven long months passed waiting for the gazette notification. Finally, on the night of 14 October, the Ministry of Public Administration published the final gazette notification for the 45th BCS. Of the 1,807 candidates recommended by the Public Service Commission (PSC), 1,702 secured jobs, while 105 were left out. Shamim Al Mahadi, Aleya Begum's son, was among those unfairly excluded from the list.

The self-reliant woman was shocked and heartbroken when she did not find her son's name in the gazette. Speaking to this correspondent over the phone, Aleya Begum raised several questions that she considered reasonable.

She said, “Let anyone from the government come and investigate our area in person. If even one person in the village can say anything bad about my son, I will have no further claim to his job. They can also enquire about him from his school, college and university teachers. If he is found innocent everywhere, why should my son be deprived despite committing no wrongdoing?”

This mother does not understand the state's complex laws or administrative calculations. But she wants the truth to come out and does not want anyone to unfairly take away a right earned through merit.

Protests by candidates excluded from the gazette, threats of ‘suicide’

Stories like that of Mahadi, Aleya Begum's son, are shared by many meritorious candidates across the country. According to the candidates, despite successfully passing every stage of the PSC examination and receiving recommendations, their names were not included in the gazette without any specific reason. None of them has been accused of any criminal offence or crime against the state.

Having lost jobs they earned through merit and a transparent process, these young people have taken to the streets, facing extreme uncertainty about their future. They are holding a sit-in programme in front of the Raju Memorial Sculpture at Dhaka University in the capital.

The candidates who say they have been deprived have issued an extreme ultimatum, threatening to ‘kill themselves’ at Shahbagh unless a supplementary gazette is published immediately to ensure their appointments.

Speaking in a tearful voice during the sit-in programme, Nur-e-Alam, one of the candidates excluded from the gazette, said, “I was recommended for the Ansar cadre in the 44th BCS and am currently working as an assistant director.

But although I was newly recommended for the police cadre in the 45th BCS, my name has now been excluded from the gazette. I received clearance for my previous job, so I want the government to explain how I was excluded this time.”

Another candidate, Moniruzzaman, was recommended for the fisheries cadre. He said, “I worked relentlessly for four to five years and passed the BCS examination. Why should I face this punishment despite committing no crime? I do not know what answer to give my parents. We are not asking anyone for mercy; we want back the job we earned through our own merit.”

The candidates have placed five demands before the government. These include announcing a specific date for issuing a revised gazette, publishing a supplementary gazette for candidates who face no legal barriers, informing candidates in writing of the reasons for their exclusion, providing them with an opportunity to defend themselves, and ensuring transparency regarding the information used to exclude candidates during administrative verification.

What is police verification, and when did it begin?

After the final results of the BCS examination are announced, candidates undergo background verification before the gazette notification is published. The practice was introduced during the 1920s under British rule. At the time, its primary purpose was to suppress anti-British movements across the Indian subcontinent and examine candidates' political beliefs and whether they were involved in any activities against the then government before recruiting them to government jobs.

According to police guidelines, the verification process is supposed to establish only whether a candidate has any specific criminal case or record of criminal activity against them. However, allegations have persisted for a long time that this century-old practice from the British colonial era is being used to block merit-based appointments on the grounds of candidates' relatives' political identities or other irrelevant information.

Experts have also expressed frustration over the longstanding bureaucratic complications surrounding the BCS, irregularities in the name of verification and political discrimination.

‘State injustice must stop immediately’

Professor Rezwana Karim Snigdha of the Department of Anthropology at Jahangirnagar University told Prothom Alo, “In an independent state, holding back the merit and future of young people through an outdated verification system inherited from the British era is a major systemic flaw. If there is no specific information about a criminal offence against a candidate or a court conviction, depriving them of an opportunity on political or other pretexts is in no way acceptable. What, then, have we learned from such a historic mass uprising in 2024?

“I would say that the old practice of political party-based discrimination has now turned into ‘discrimination based on beliefs’. When the government runs the state, it cannot afford to harbour prejudice against any particular party, group or community. Doing so amounts to a breach of its oath. Depriving candidates who have demonstrated their merit of their rightful government jobs is a form of ‘state-structural corruption’. This state injustice must stop immediately,” she added.

State minister for public administration assures re-verification

Regarding the overall situation, State Minister for Public Administration Md Abdul Bari told Prothom Alo, “Verification is a regular part of the government recruitment process. It has always been there. It is nothing new. More than half of the candidates whose names did not appear in the gazette were temporarily excluded because of shortcomings in their required documents and other legal papers. The cases of the remaining candidates whose names were not included have come to our attention. The prime minister has given clear instructions that no citizen of the country should be deprived of their rightful entitlements under the state's laws and regulations."

“Therefore, an initiative will be taken to re-examine (re-verify) all the information concerning the candidates who were excluded. Everyone who is considered eligible for the job within the legal framework will be appointed. You have already seen in the 49th BCS that even after the publication of the final gazette, eligible candidates secured jobs through re-verification,” he added.

item.title: Japan to invest Tk 774.7 billion in Bangladesh
item.description:
Japan will invest one trillion yen, or USD 6.35 billion, in Bangladesh’s private sector over the next five years. The amount is equivalent to Tk 774.7 billion, calculated at an exchange rate of Tk 122 to the dollar.

Japan’s Nikkei Asia reported the development on Thursday. Reuters also published a report citing the Nikkei Asia article.

According to the report, the Japanese government has agreed to arrange the funds for investment in Bangladesh’s private sector. The investment is expected to be announced in a joint statement following a summit meeting between Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

PM’s Japan visit: Reducing metro rail costs, loan interest rates likely to be discussed

Nikkei Asia reported that the announcement primarily aims to strengthen economic cooperation with Bangladesh and reduce China’s influence in Asia. Another objective is to establish Bangladesh as an investment hub.

The Japanese investment will be used in the automobile industry, other manufacturing sectors, and infrastructure development in the power and energy sectors. Japanese companies will also invest in the Bangladesh Special Economic Zone, developed through initiatives involving Japanese trading house Sumitomo Corporation and other partners.

Japan signed an economic partnership agreement with Bangladesh in February.

Ambassador to stay away from Tokyo during PM's Japan visit, ministry secretary sent to coordinate

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will visit Japan on 26 October for a four-day trip. On the second day of the visit, 27 October, he will hold bilateral talks with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi at her office. He will also attend a dinner hosted in his honour by the Japanese prime minister.

Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam said the visit would include discussions on expanding access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market, increasing Japanese investment and strengthening business ties.

At a press briefing at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday, he said discussions were under way on around eight memorandums of understanding (MoU) with Japan covering cooperation in agriculture, fisheries, human resource development and skills training, civil aviation and other sectors.

Several MoUs likely to be announced during PM's visit to Japan

Officials hope to sign three or four of the memorandums, he added.

The foreign secretary also expressed hope that the visit would create opportunities to expand cooperation in emerging areas, including renewable energy, the environment, science, technology, digital innovation, research and human resource development.

Japan is one of Bangladesh’s major development partners. It has supported the construction and implementation of several important infrastructure and connectivity projects, including the metro rail system, the third terminal at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and the Matarbari deep-sea port.

item.title: Rivers swallow evidence, leaving murders unsolved Evidence of crime drifts with the current
item.description:
On 23 August, river police recovered the bodies of a woman, a child, a young man and a young woman from the Buriganga in Dhaka within a span of six hours. Black cloth was wrapped around the woman’s neck, while the child’s body was wrapped in a scarf.

The young man and woman had their hands tied together, and both had visible injuries. Police suspect they were murdered and their bodies dumped in the river to conceal the crimes. As their identities could not be established, all four bodies were buried as unidentified persons 11 days later.

Earlier, on 30 April last year, police recovered the body of an unidentified woman from a river in Narayanganj. A scarf had been wrapped around a bamboo pole beside the body. The woman was naked. She was buried as an unidentified person in the area. Her relatives later identified her after seeing photographs kept at the police station. The investigation revealed that she had been murdered. One person arrested in connection with the case subsequently gave a confessional statement in court.

River police recovered 2,064 bodies from rivers across Bangladesh between January 2021 and December 2025, a period of five years. Another 430 bodies were recovered between January and September this year. In total, 2,494 bodies were recovered over five years and nine months.

The bodies included victims of murder, people who accidentally fell into rivers and drowned, and people who died by suicide after jumping into the water.

River police officials say criminals dump bodies in rivers after committing murders to destroy evidence and evade arrest. They consider rivers a “safe place” to dispose of bodies and conceal their crimes.

The overall picture over five years and nine months

According to statistics from the River Police Headquarters, more men than women were among the bodies recovered between January 2021 and September this year. The remains of women and children were also found.

During this period, 392 murder cases were filed at police stations across the country, along with 26 cases involving suicide by jumping into rivers. Other deaths occurred while people were fishing, travelling or bathing, as well as in natural disasters and boat accidents. A total of 2,077 cases of unnatural death were filed.

According to figures provided by the River Police Headquarters, 1,739 of the recovered bodies were identified, while the identities of 755 remain unknown.

Cases are filed at the relevant police stations based on evidence found on recovered bodies. Bodies whose identities cannot be established are buried as unidentified persons by Anjuman Mufidul Islam, a charitable organisation.

DNA samples are collected from all recovered bodies, and photographs are taken and kept at the relevant police stations. If someone subsequently visits a police station and identifies a body after its burial, the police take steps to advance the case and further investigation based on the identification and other findings.

2021–25: 2,064 bodies recovered in five years

According to River Police Headquarters data, 318 bodies were recovered in 2021, 360 in 2022, 405 in 2023, 440 in 2024 and 541 in 2025. This brought the total to 2,064 over the five years. Murder cases were filed in 335 incidents in which the deaths were identified as homicides.

The number of bodies recovered increased every year during this period, reaching its highest level in 2025.

First nine months of this year: 430 bodies recovered

Of the 430 bodies recovered between January and September this year, 314 people were identified. The remaining 116 were buried as unidentified persons by Anjuman Mufidul Islam.

During these nine months, 57 murder cases were filed in connection with recovered bodies.

The police data also recorded 116 deaths while bathing, 57 while travelling or visiting places, 38 in boat accidents, 37 while fishing, 19 after falling from watercraft, two in natural disasters and one after jumping into a river. These categories accounted for 270 deaths.

The cause of death of another 104 people could not be determined, according to police data. Cases of unnatural death were filed in these instances.

Regional breakdown

River police have divided the country's waterways into 11 regions: Dhaka, Narayanganj, Chattogram, Chandpur, Barishal, Faridpur, Kishoreganj, Rajshahi, Tangail, Khulna and Sylhet.

The Dhaka region covers the Buriganga, the Balu River near Khilkhet, part of the Shitalakkhya, the Padma near Dohar and the Meghna near Narsingdi.

Regional data are available from January 2023 to September 2026. Over these three years and nine months, the highest number of bodies—398—were recovered in the Dhaka region, followed by Narayanganj with 253. Sylhet recorded the lowest number, at 20.

During the same period, 211 bodies were recovered in Barishal, 177 in Rajshahi, 167 in Chattogram, 149 in Faridpur, 127 each in Chandpur and Khulna, 94 in Kishoreganj and 93 in Tangail.

Dhaka also recorded the highest number of recoveries during the first nine months of this year, with 78 bodies. Barishal ranked second with 63, followed by Narayanganj with 60, Rajshahi with 55, Faridpur with 50, Tangail with 29, Khulna with 23, and Chattogram, Chandpur and Kishoreganj with 22 each. Six bodies were recovered in Sylhet.

Unidentified bodies hamper investigations

River police officials say many bodies have already begun decomposing before they surface. Fingerprints disappear and faces become disfigured, making identification difficult. Sometimes, only human skeletons are recovered.

Even when a post-mortem examination establishes evidence of murder, investigators may be unable to bring the perpetrators to justice if the victim's identity remains unknown. In other cases, the identity may eventually be established through various means, but decomposition makes it impossible to determine the cause of death.

Of the four bodies recovered from the Buriganga on 23 August, the body of a 30-year-old woman and that of a child aged three to four were found on the riverbank near the Mirerbag Cold Storage area in Keraniganj. The bodies of the young man and woman were recovered near Madaripur Ghat in Kalindi. All four bodies had begun decomposing. As no one came forward to claim them, Anjuman Mufidul Islam buried them as unidentified persons 11 days later.

Abdullah Al Mamun, superintendent of police for the Dhaka region of the River Police, told Prothom Alo that the killers had dumped the bodies in the river to conceal their crimes.

Two murder cases have been filed: one at South Keraniganj Police Station over the bodies of the woman and child, and another at Keraniganj Model Police Station over the bodies of the young man and woman. Photographs and DNA samples have been preserved. If anyone approaches the police stations looking for the missing individuals, investigators will attempt to establish their identities through DNA matching, he said.

Identity established through photographs and socks

On 16 January last year, river police recovered a man's body from the Shitalakkhya River in Narayanganj. The body was sent to the morgue at Narayanganj General Hospital for a post-mortem examination. The Kachpur River Police kept photographs of the body. As his identity could not be established, he was buried through Anjuman Mufidul Islam.

Later, his son Mahbubur Rahman identified the body as that of his father, Jabbar Hawlader, 45, by examining the photographs preserved by the police and the socks on the deceased man's feet. Jabbar worked as an autorickshaw driver. Mahbubur subsequently filed a murder case against unidentified individuals at Siddhirganj Police Station.

The investigation was assigned to Mainul Islam, a sub-inspector at the Kachpur River Police outpost. He is now serving at the River Police outpost under Bandar Police Station in Narayanganj.

Mainul Islam told Prothom Alo that the family had informed him that Jabbar had left home to drive his autorickshaw on 13 January last year and never returned. He had taken his mobile phone with him.

Following a lead from the phone, police detained a young man named Al Amin. During questioning, Al Amin said that a man named Shawon had sold him the phone.

Police subsequently detained and questioned Shawon. According to Mainul Islam, Shawon confessed to the murder and said that, after evening, he had lured Jabbar into consuming a soft drink mixed with an intoxicating substance and high-dose sleeping pills to render him unconscious, intending to steal his autorickshaw.

Jabbar was then removed from the autorickshaw while unconscious and thrown into the river from Adamjee Ghat in Narayanganj. Seven people shared the proceeds from the sale of the autorickshaw and the mobile phone, according to the account.

Mainul Islam said seven people involved in the crime had been arrested. Police recovered Jabbar's autorickshaw and mobile phone from them. Four of the accused gave confessional statements in court. They were members of an organised autorickshaw theft and robbery gang.

What post-mortem examinations reveal

River police sources say cases of unnatural death are generally filed when a body recovered from a river shows no signs of injury or has decomposed. However, if the condition of the body, physical evidence and surrounding circumstances suggest anything suspicious, river police file a murder case at the relevant police station, even if the victim's identity is unknown.

If an investigation and post-mortem examination establish that a death was a homicide, the case initially filed as an unnatural death is converted into a murder case, which the river police then investigate.

According to River Police Headquarters, post-mortem reports in confirmed homicide cases have cited rape, strangulation, head injuries and death caused by being thrown into water. River police have also recovered bodies with severed or injured hands, legs, necks and other body parts, as well as bodies wrapped in sacks. Murder cases are filed in such incidents.

Professor Mostaque Rahim, president of the Medicolegal Society of Bangladesh, told Prothom Alo that bodies recovered from rivers are often decomposed. Even when injuries or cuts are visible, decomposition can destroy crucial evidence. Fish and insects feeding on the bodies can also damage evidence, making it difficult to establish the cause of death.

In hot weather, bodies of people who have drowned may surface within 24 hours. If recovered at that stage, the cause of death can often be determined, he said.

Professor Mostaque Rahim added that the forensic medicine departments of government medical colleges in Bangladesh lacked modern equipment and laboratories. Establishing such facilities would help forensic experts assess deaths even when bodies had decomposed and determine the precise cause of death.

River police sources also said they collect general diaries (GDs) filed at police stations across the country concerning missing persons and investigate them with particular attention. Leads from these reports sometimes result in bodies being recovered from rivers.

Surveillance at river ghats and other potential dumping sites

Mohammad Rezaul Karim, additional inspector general of the River Police, told Prothom Alo that the circumstances surrounding a death cannot be unravelled if the victim's identity remains unknown.

Information obtained from investigations into murder cases involving bodies recovered from rivers indicates that killings are motivated by business disputes, family conflicts, disputes over drug trafficking, extramarital relationships and vehicle theft. After committing the murders, perpetrators dump the bodies in rivers to prevent identification, he said.

Asked why more bodies are recovered in the Dhaka and Narayanganj regions, the River Police chief said Dhaka, Narayanganj and Munshiganj are among the country's most densely populated areas. Business activity and employment opportunities are also concentrated there, and crime levels are correspondingly higher.

Asked what measures could prevent criminals from dumping bodies in rivers, Additional IGP Rezaul Karim said perpetrators often dispose of bodies in remote, isolated locations. The bodies subsequently drift with the current and are eventually recovered.

Police are analysing the waterways to identify the points used to dump bodies. Intelligence surveillance is being maintained around the clock at river ghats, riverside markets and roads. Several potential dumping sites, including Adamjee Ghat in Narayanganj, have been identified, and intelligence surveillance and patrols have been stepped up there, he said.

According to River Police data, Bangladesh has approximately 7,500 kilometres of navigable waterways during the monsoon, shrinking to around 4,500 kilometres in the dry season. Of this, approximately 3,500 kilometres are regularly used by watercraft. Ensuring security across this extensive network of waterways remains a major challenge for the River Police.

Professor Muhammad Umar Faruk of the Department of Criminology and Police Science at Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University in Tangail told Prothom Alo that professional criminals had come to regard waterways as safe places to dispose of bodies.

After rape and murder, perpetrators deliberately and carefully dump bodies into rivers from secluded locations to conceal their crimes. Such incidents are increasing, he said. Rivers have also been used to dispose of bodies following politically motivated killings at various times.

Professor Umar Faruk said criminals assume that even if a body surfaces, it will have decomposed and drifted from one place to another with the current. They believe the victim will remain unidentified and be buried as an unclaimed person.

To solve such cases, investigators must conduct thorough inquiries, gathering circumstantial evidence and applying psychological insight, he said. The criminologist recommended identifying potential dumping sites, increasing law enforcement surveillance and installing CCTV cameras to prevent bodies from being disposed of in rivers.

item.description:
Bangladesh have announced their squad for the first match of their two-Test series against the West Indies. Fast bowler Nahid Rana has again been left out because of injury.

Soumya Sarkar, who was in the squad for the one-off Test against Afghanistan, has not been included. Fast bowler Khaled Ahmed has also been dropped. Taskin Ahmed, who was rested for the Afghanistan Test, has returned to the squad.

Bangladesh crash out of tri-series after defeat to Afghanistan

In Nahid Rana’s absence, Hasan Mahmud and Taskin will lead Bangladesh’s pace attack. They will be joined by Shoriful Islam and Ebadot Hossain. All four have been included in the squad for the first Test under captain Najmul Hossain.

Nahid Rana suffered a side strain while playing T20 cricket during the Zimbabwe series in July. The injury ruled him out of the two-Test series against Australia.

He was also left out of the one-off Test against Afghanistan because he had not completed his rehabilitation. During rehabilitation, he developed fresh pain in his hip, ruling him out of this Test as well.

World Test Championship: The standings and Bangladesh’s chances

Soumya did not get an opportunity to play against Afghanistan. He had also been included in the squad for the Australia series but did not get a chance to play there either. He has now been dropped without playing a match.

Towhid Hridoy has retained his place in the Test squad. He, too, did not get an opportunity to take the field against Afghanistan.

Off-spinner Nayeem Hasan has also been included in the squad for the first Test against the West Indies, alongside Taijul Islam and Mehidy Hasan Miraz, who retain their places.

Bangladesh suffer 99-run defeat to Zimbabwe in tri-nation series opener

item.title: Why is Charmonai Pir visiting the US for the first time?
item.description:
Mufti Syed Muhammad Rezaul Karim, amir of Islami Andolan Bangladesh, has travelled to the United States for the first time. Party leaders describe the visit as a religious outreach tour. However, they also see it as an opportunity to raise the party’s profile internationally.

Meanwhile, some social media users have criticised the visit, linking it to a remark made several months ago by the party’s Senior Nayeb-e-Amir Faizul Karim, about a “caravan heading towards America”.

Rezaul Karim, widely known as the Pir of Charmonai, left Dhaka for the United States on an Emirates flight on the evening of 13 October. According to party sources, he is on a 14-day visit at the invitation of the An Nur Foundation.

Party leaders believe the visit could help raise Islami Andolan’s international profile. They say that although Jamaat-e-Islami is known outside Bangladesh, particularly in Western countries, as a religion-based political party, Islami Andolan has not gained similar recognition.

During the tour, he is meeting expatriate Bangladeshis in various US states and delivering religious talks at mosques and Muslim community gatherings. His schedule also includes meetings with businesspeople and leaders of various international organisations.

According to Islami Andolan leaders, Rezaul Karim is better known in the United States as the Pir of Charmonai than as the party’s amir. He is building connections with followers of Sufism from different countries. He is also taking part in religious discussions and outreach programmes, at their invitation.

Party leaders believe the visit could help raise Islami Andolan’s international profile. They say that although Jamaat-e-Islami is known outside Bangladesh, particularly in Western countries, as a religion-based political party, Islami Andolan has not gained similar recognition.

Jamaat presents us as extremists at US Embassy: Charmonai pir

They hope the visit will help bridge that gap while creating an opportunity to present the practices and philosophy of Sufi Islam.

Islami Andolan secretary general Gazi Ataur Rahman told Prothom Alo that the Pir of Charmonai had travelled to the United States at the invitation of the An Nur Foundation. It is his first visit to the country. Followers of Islami Andolan, as well as people associated with other parties, are attending his religious talks there, he said.

Party sources said Rezaul Karim had previously visited Saudi Arabia and several other Muslim countries.

Criticism over Faizul Karim’s remarks

Criticism of the Pir of Charmonai’s visit to the United States has drawn attention to a remark made by Islami Andolan’s senior Nayeb-e-Amir Mufti Syed Muhammad Faizul Karim.

At a conference in Gournadi, Barishal, on 22 July to mark the founding anniversary of Islami Jubo Andolan, he spoke about forming a political alliance in support of Islam.

Mufti Syed Muhammad Faizul Karim, senior nayeb-e-amir, Islami Andolan We were heading towards Medina. But the steering wheel was hijacked; it was robbed. Our caravan was heading towards Medina, but suddenly I saw it heading towards America. Followers of Medina cannot go to America.

Faizul Karim said Islami Andolan had formed an alliance with the aim of creating a common electoral symbol in support of Islam, led by the Pir of Charmonai.

He added, “We were heading towards Medina. But the steering wheel was hijacked; it was robbed. Our caravan was heading towards Medina, but suddenly I saw it heading towards America. Followers of Medina cannot go to America.”

Following the Pir of Charmonai’s visit to the United States, some social media users have criticised him by drawing a connection between the trip and those remarks.

Maulana Fakhruddin Ahmad, central assistant secretary of Bangladesh Majlisul Mufassirin, wrote on his Facebook page on 14 October. “Is the Pir Sahib of Charmonai really going on a visit to America? Has he, then, turned towards America? That is precisely the accusation he makes against Jamaat.”

Islami Andolan leaders, however, consider the criticism unjustified. They argue that travelling to the United States or conducting religious activities there does not mean accepting the country’s state policies or political ideology.

Gazi Ataur Rahman told Prothom Alo that there was no basis for concluding that the Pir of Charmonai had adopted US policies simply because he had travelled there. He was not making political statements in the country but encouraging people in matters of religion, the party’s secretary general said.

Activities during the visit

Rezaul Karim arrived at John F Kennedy International Airport in New York on 14 October. He was received by Sardar Barkatullah, president of Darul Uloom New York, Mufti Mizanur Rahman Saeed, the institution’s chief faqih, and Maulana Azir Uddin, chief imam of Baitul Aman Jame Mosque.

According to his itinerary, the Pir of Charmonai attended an event at the American Muslim Center on 14 October. The following day, he delivered an Islami Bayan (religious sermon focused on moral and spiritual reform) at Port Washington Mosque.

Rezaul Karim arrived at John F Kennedy International Airport in New York on 14 October. He was received by Sardar Barkatullah, president of Darul Uloom New York, Mufti Mizanur Rahman Saeed, the institution’s chief faqih, and Maulana Azir Uddin, chief imam of Baitul Aman Jame Mosque.

On 16 October, he delivered the Friday sermon and led prayers at Jalalabad Jame Mosque in New Jersey. On the same day, he also spoke at a waaz mahfil (religious gathering featuring sermons) at Baitul Aman Islamic Center.

Mufti Rezaul Karim has also taken part in religious sermons and special waaz and prayer gatherings at the Bronx Muslim Center, Bangladesh Muslim Center Jame Mosque, Masjid Al-Aman Inc in Brooklyn, Sanai Party Hall in Jackson Heights, Buffalo and Masjid Quba.

He is also scheduled to attend various religious events at Darul Uloom in New York, Masjidun Noor in Michigan and the An Nur Cultural Center.

item.title: Apratim murder: Two of the four accused are minors; father seeks highest punishment
item.description:
Police have submitted a chargesheet to the court in the murder case of Ishayat Shahriar, also known as Apratim (13), the son of Nahida Begum, an associate professor in the Department of Bengali at Cumilla University. Four people, including two adolescents, have been named in the chargesheet.

The chargesheet against the four accused was submitted last Tuesday, 31 days after Apratim’s body was recovered. His family is now awaiting the start of the trial. They hope the judicial process will be completed swiftly and that the perpetrators will receive the maximum punishment.

Lutfur Rahman, additional superintendent of police and media officer for the district police, confirmed the submission of the charge sheet at around 12:30 am early Thursday. He said a chargesheet had been filed in court on 20 October against four accused, including two adolescents. The investigation had found preliminary evidence of criminal involvement against all four.

Speaking to Prothom Alo at around 1 am early Thursday, KM Firoz Shahriar, the plaintiff in the case and Apratim’s father, said, “Three days ago, I called the case’s investigating officer to ask, ‘When will you submit the chargesheet to the court?’ He told me that the chargesheet would be submitted as soon as the Puja holidays ended. At around 12:30 am today (last night), he called me and informed me that he had submitted the chargesheet to the court. They have notified me of the matter. Beyond that, I know nothing more.”

Firoz Shahriar added, “Our lives revolved around Apratim. But they have taken that away from us. We want to see the murderers brought to trial without delay. We hope the court will impose the highest punishment on the killers as soon as possible. Now we have only one demand: the maximum punishment for the killers.”

Names of the four accused

Inspector (Investigation) Rajib Ahmed of Cumilla Sadar South Model Police Station investigated the case. He was the second investigating officer assigned to it.

The charge sheet names Saiful Islam, also known as Tuhin (19); Md. Siam (19); and two adolescents aged 15 and 16 as accused. They have been charged under Sections 302, 201 and 34 of the Penal Code. In accordance with the Children Act, the two adolescents have been identified as children in the chargesheet.

According to police, Tuhin was the main planner of the murder and the principal accused. Siam was also involved in planning Apratim’s murder. Three people are accused of directly participating in the killing, while Siam allegedly provided assistance, police said.

Police stated that Tuhin and the two adolescents aged 15 and 16 had given confessional statements before the court. The other accused, Siam, has also been charged with assisting in and participating in the planning of the murder.

The details of the chargesheet are still unclear to Apratim’s family. They have had questions about the ages of the two adolescents from the very beginning. The family had demanded that their actual ages be determined through DNA testing, if necessary. Teachers and students at Cumilla University had also raised questions on the matter. After receiving a copy of the chargesheet, the family plans to consult a lawyer and consider further legal action.

Additional Superintendent of Police Md. Lutfur Rahman said last night that the chargesheet had been submitted to the court within the deadline set by the superintendent of police. The accused were arrested within 24 hours of the recovery of the body, and the investigation was completed with due diligence, leading to the submission of the charge sheet within 31 days, he said.

However, because of the government holidays for Durga Puja, further court proceedings did not begin immediately after the chargesheet was filed. According to police sources, although the charge sheet was submitted on 20 October, court proceedings are expected to resume on Sunday after the holidays.

How Apratim was murdered

Apratim went missing on 18 September after leaving his home in the Gandhamati area of Kotbari, Cumilla city. He was a seventh-grade student at Border Guard Public School in Kotbari. The following day, 19 September, police recovered his body from an isolated wooded area in the Lalmai Hills in Sananda village, under Bijoypur union of Sadar South upazila.

According to police, Apratim was deliberately taken to the secluded woodland with the intention of snatching the iPhone he had with him. When he resisted the attempt to take his mobile phone, he was struck on the head with a bamboo stick. He died as a result.

During the investigation, police initially arrested three people, including Tuhin, the principal accused. Later, police said they had found evidence of Siam’s involvement in the crime and arrested him as well. Police had stated that, based on information provided by Tuhin, Apratim’s iPhone was recovered from beneath the mattress on a bed at Tuhin’s home.

After Apratim went missing, police reviewed CCTV footage from various locations and said they had identified Tuhin. According to police, questioning him led to information about the involvement of others in the murder.

item.title: Why do Bangladeshi immigrants take this position on Alberta’s independence issue?
item.description:
On the night of 19 October, as ballot boxes were opened at more than 1,400 polling stations across Alberta, Bangladeshi immigrants across Canada watched their television screens with bated breath. The unofficial results were in: Alberta was not leaving Canada.

With unofficial results from approximately 86 per cent of polling stations counted, 75.3 per cent of votes were cast in favor of “unity,” while 24.7 percent supported separation. The margin exceeded 960,000 votes. In urban areas such as Calgary-Elbow, “unity” received 85 per cent of the vote. The margin was comparatively narrower in rural Alberta. Immigrants do not live in rural areas. The results made one thing clear: it was immigrants who ensured that Canada would never be allowed to break apart.

The votes of nearly all immigrants, including Bangladeshi immigrants, went against Alberta’s independence. About a week before the referendum, an Albertan colleague of mine asked: “If Bangladesh’s independence in 1971 was justified in the eyes of Bangladeshis, why are the aspirations of Alberta or Quebec unjustified?” Everyone interested in seeing Alberta separate from Canada knows that, on average, 90-95 percent of diaspora communities oppose the breakup of Canada.

The tenth question on the ballot was the real issue: Would Alberta remain a province of Canada, or would the provincial government initiate the legal process, in accordance with the Constitution, to hold a “binding” referendum on secession?

On 30 October 1995, French-speaking Quebec came close to becoming independent as well. Voter turnout in the referendum was 94 per cent, the highest in Canadian history. The “No” side, opposing separation, won by just 50.58 percent of the vote. The “Yes” side lost with 49.42 per cent. The margin was a mere 54,000 votes. A group of voters roughly equivalent in size to the crowd at a large stadium had prevented the province from breaking away. That very night, Premier Jacques Parizeau blamed immigrant voters for the defeat.

That statement still rankles in the memories of immigrants in Canada. Diaspora communities did not take kindly to an immigrant citizen’s vote being singled out as a “problem.” Yet the incident did not fuel anti-immigrant politics.

Alberta is proof of how rewarding democracy can be when it is truly democratic. Premier Danielle Smith had worked tirelessly to make Alberta independent and had called the referendum. After the votes were counted, she herself reaffirmed Alberta’s place in a united Canada. She respected the people’s verdict.

2.

Let us return to my colleague’s question and seek an answer: Why do the people of a nation that won its own independence in 1971 at the cost of blood oppose Alberta’s independence?

The answer lies in the referendum results. All five questions on the ballot concerned immigration. All five passed, with support ranging from 54 to 64 per cent. Discriminatory demands prevailed, including giving the province control over immigration; restricting provincially funded healthcare, education, and social services to citizens, permanent residents, and people with status approved by Alberta; and charging fees for services provided to people with temporary status. In fact, nearly 100 per cent of the votes cast by non-immigrants were in favour of tighter immigration controls.

A person who has lost their home and land to river erosion knows how devastating it is to hear the ground crumble beneath their feet. Someone who has left behind family, friends, and loved ones to find shelter on new soil does not want cracks to appear in that new home, too. In 1971, the Biharis stood against the breakup of Pakistan for the same reason. Breaking the bonds of their homeland, the scent of its soil and the deep attachment to the place that had nurtured them like a mother, they had arrived in a foreign country with nothing. They had not come there only to become uprooted all over again.

Two. I found an answer to my colleague’s question in Allen Buchanan’s book Secession: The Morality of Political Divorce. Buchanan explains the issue through the concept of “remedial secession.” A moral right to secede arises only as a remedy for serious injustices, such as genocide, systematic discrimination, or the complete denial of political voice. In its 1998 interpretation of international law, the Supreme Court of Canada expressed a position broadly similar to this. The right to self-determination belongs to colonized or oppressed peoples who are denied a fair opportunity to exercise self-determination within the state.

Bangladesh meets Buchanan’s criteria. The denial of the mother tongue in 1952, the trampling of an overwhelming popular mandate in the 1970 election, the dark night of 25 March, and nine months of genocide made independence the only option.

Alberta has its own legislature, constitutional ownership of its resources, and full representation in Ottawa. The current prime minister himself grew up in Edmonton. Quebec enjoys constitutional protection for the French language, its own immigration agreements, and its own civil law system. There is resentment, and there are allegations of injustice. But there is no inhumanity, exploitation, or deprivation on that scale.

Three. Like immigrants from other countries, Bangladeshi immigrants make the same argument: the oath we took was to Canada. Our passports are Canadian. Immigration, permanent resident status, and permits for students and temporary workers all fall under federal jurisdiction. Section 6 of the Charter grants us the right to live and work anywhere in the country. In an independent Alberta or Quebec, all of these rights and arrangements would suddenly have been thrown into uncertainty and a legal vacuum.

Four. One Alberta independence supporter proposed creating an “Albertan citizenship.” He said citizenship would be determined “on the basis of the decision of those who win the referendum.” Avnish Nanda, an immigration lawyer in Edmonton, had therefore warned that if Alberta became independent, there would be no guarantee of freedom and status for its new citizens. Immigrants who have already left their countries, abandoned their languages, lost recognition of their professional qualifications, and started from scratch are unlikely to risk being reduced to “zero” a second time. That is only natural.

Five. Another reason immigrants voted “No” was their fear that immigration would be restricted. The five referendum questions on immigration restrictions themselves demonstrate this concern. Why would diaspora communities vote “Yes” in a political climate that seeks to label them as “outsiders”?

Six. On 8 October 1971, Pierre Trudeau declared multiculturalism a state policy in Canada. Later, Section 27 of the Charter and the Multiculturalism Act of 1988 gave it a constitutional foundation. This model upholds minority rights and liberal democracy together.

The views of the 500,000 citizens who favour separation are equally legitimate. Alberta makes one of the largest contributions to Canada’s economy. However, the benefits of those contributions are used to develop less prosperous provinces

Pierre Trudeau was among the first Western leaders to speak out in support of Bangladesh’s independence. Bangladeshi immigrants feel a deep, emotional and psychological sense of gratitude toward Canada and love the country for it. In their eyes, the provinces are like brothers. Why should they separate?

Seven. Bangladeshi immigrants viewed the situation as akin to taking a saw to a boat in the middle of a storm and cutting it into pieces. The US tariff war, threats to turn Canada into the “51st state,” and contacts between people close to the US administration and Alberta separatists all suggest that secession would narrow the space Canada provides as a refuge for immigrants. In the eyes of immigrants, creating a new fracture within the country at a dangerous time is like handing the keys to one’s home to a thief.

3.

The province’s resentment began in 1980, prompted by Pierre Trudeau’s National Energy Program. In reaction to Ottawa’s control over Alberta’s oil resources, Gordon Kesler of the separatist Western Canada Concept party won the Olds-Didsbury by-election in 1982. Since then, the movement has experienced various ups and downs, giving rise to different factions and opposing positions.

The views of the 500,000 citizens who favour separation are equally legitimate. Alberta makes one of the largest contributions to Canada’s economy. However, the benefits of those contributions are used to develop less prosperous provinces. Since 1965, wealthy Alberta has received no benefits from the federal equalisation program. Yet for decades, it has been among the biggest contributors to Canada’s economy.

Pipelines, carbon policy, the energy sector—in every area, the province is subject to Ottawa’s intervention.

Will anti-immigrant sentiment increase following the defeat of Alberta’s separatists? Only time will tell. However, an analysis of historical patterns gives reason to believe that anti-immigrant sentiment will never become a cause for serious concern in Canada. Canada is not merely constitutionally committed to humanitarian values; it is also one of the world’s most humane countries in practice. The triumph of humanity comes before everything else in this country.

* Helal Mohiuddin Professor of Liberal Arts, Mayville State University, North Dakota, USA

item.title: Italy, Greece, and Cyprus send back 35 Bangladeshis
item.description:
Three European countries have repatriated 35 Bangladeshis. Of them, 19 returned from Italy, 10 from Greece and six from Cyprus.

Immigration police and airport sources said the 35 Bangladeshis arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at 8:15 am today, Friday, on a chartered special flight (PVG 9445).

With support from Civil Aviation Security and the Expatriate Welfare Desk at the airport, BRAC’s Migration Programme provided the returnees with emergency assistance, counselling and financial support to help them reach their respective homes.

Bangladeshis among 79 migrants rescued off Greece’s Crete island

Representatives from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the European Union were also present there at the time.

Asked about the return of the 35 Bangladeshis, Shariful Hasan, associate director of BRAC Migration Programme and the BRAC Youth Platform, told Prothom Alo that 19 Bangladeshis from Italy, 10 from Greece and six from Cyprus returned on a special flight.

All of them received assistance at the airport through the Prottasha-2 project, jointly funded by the European Union and BRAC. They will later receive counselling and training, followed by financial assistance, he said.

In 2017, the Bangladesh government signed standard operating procedure (SOP) agreements with European countries to facilitate the repatriation of undocumented or irregular Bangladeshis from Europe.

Coordinated action needed to rehabilitate returning migrants

Since then, around 5,000 Bangladeshis have returned under the agreements. The largest numbers have returned from Cyprus, Italy, Romania and France.

Shariful Hasan said that over the past few years, the largest numbers of returnees from Europe had come from Italy, Greece and Germany. Those who return receive emergency assistance and counselling at the airport, followed by financial support to help them rebuild their lives.

At the same time, awareness campaigns are being conducted across the country to discourage people from taking risks to reach Europe. The government has also stepped up initiatives to facilitate the legal recruitment of workers from Bangladesh by European countries, he added.

item.title: Around 7,500 Bangladeshis in Saudi prisons; government seeks copies of death sentences against two citizens
item.description:
Around 7,500 Bangladeshis are being held in prisons across Saudi Arabia, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam has said. She also said Bangladesh had written to the Saudi government seeking copies of the court verdicts to obtain details about the execution of two Bangladeshi nationals. The government has yet to receive detailed information about the two men.

The body of Bangladeshi worker Md Shahed Ahmed, who was killed in an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the Saudi capital, arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka on Friday morning. The state minister went to the airport to receive the body and made these remarks in response to questions from journalists.

Shahed Ahmed’s body arrived in Dhaka shortly after 8:00am. His body, along with government assistance, were subsequently handed over to his wife, Kohinur Akter Kakoli.

The state minister said Bangladesh had sought details from the Saudi ambassador about the execution of the two Bangladeshis. The government had formally requested copies of the court verdicts from Saudi Arabia. Once the documents are received, Bangladesh will be able to learn more about what happened, she added.

Responding to a journalist’s question, Shama Obaed Islam said the Saudi government periodically sends lists of people who have been convicted of various offences or are in prison. The government is checking whether the names of the two persons appear on those lists.

Saudi Arabia airport attack: Identity of 2 injured Bangladeshis confirmed
Bangladeshis among 59 foreigners executed in Saudi Arabia in first 6 months

Noting that every country has its own legal framework and judicial system, the state minister said Bangladesh did not intend to interfere in another country’s judicial process. However, she said, it was important for Bangladesh to obtain detailed information whenever a Bangladeshi citizen is convicted abroad or executed.

Shama Obaed Islam also said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs could not resolve such matters on its own. The Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, the Ministry of Home Affairs and other relevant ministries work together on these issues, particularly where legal matters are involved.

When information emerges that a Bangladeshi citizen has been convicted abroad, the government contacts the authorities concerned through diplomatic channels. Discussions are also held on whether there is any scope for a sentence to be commuted, she added.

Execution of 2 Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia: What does the consulate’s letter say?

Shahed was the 11th

Bangladeshi worker Md Shahed Ahmed was killed in an attack by the Houthi armed group at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October. His home was in Shahjahanpur upazila of Bogura.

The state minister said more than four million Bangladeshis work in Saudi Arabia, leaving them at risk of being killed or injured if war or other accidents occur there.

Over the past six months, the bodies of 11 Bangladeshis killed in conflicts in the Middle East have been brought back to the country. Shahed was the 11th, she said.

Three Bangladeshis have been killed in missile attacks in Saudi Arabia over the past month, according to the state minister. One of their bodies arrived in Bangladesh on Friday, while efforts were under way to bring the others home as soon as possible.

Shama Obaed Islam said the government did not want any more Bangladeshi citizens to lose their lives in such circumstances. She prayed for an end to the war in the Middle East and for people of all nationalities to be spared such brutal attacks.

She also said discussions were under way with Saudi Arabia on extending or renewing the visas of migrant workers stranded in Bangladesh because of the conflict in the Middle East.

Action to be taken if complaints against missions are substantiated

Asked about complaints that Bangladeshis living abroad do not receive adequate assistance from the country’s embassies and diplomatic missions, Shama Obaed Islam said every Bangladeshi mission abroad has a labour welfare wing. Expatriate workers generally submit their complaints to these wings, where officials responsible for expatriates’ welfare or labour affairs work.

The state minister said it was the responsibility of diplomatic missions and the government to assist expatriates. If any negligence by a mission is found, it will be investigated and the necessary action will be taken.

Shahed Ahmed was killed in the attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on 10 October. His home was in Madla village of Shahjahanpur upazila, Bogura. His father is Md Rafiqul Islam and his mother is Shahera Begum.

Shahed worked as a plumber on a project in Jeddah for a Saudi contracting company. He had a valid Saudi residence and work permit, known as an iqama. After taking leave to attend his brother’s funeral, he was returning to his workplace in Jeddah via Riyadh. He was at Riyadh airport when the attack took place.

Two Bangladeshis, including Shahed, were killed in the attack. The other victim was Md Nasrullah Badarpuri, from Badarpur village in Nangalkot upazila of Cumilla. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs had said at the time that another 24 Bangladeshis were injured in the incident.

item.title: Baul music event cancelled in Sunamganj over objections to female performers
item.description:
A private Baul music event in the home area of Baul legend Shah Abdul Karim was not allowed to go ahead after objections were raised that it could involve “obscenity in the name of music”.

A written application was also submitted to the police seeking cancellation of the event. The organiser later cancelled it to avoid any unpleasant situation. The event had been scheduled for Thursday.

The incident took place in Hatia village of Kulanj Union in Dirai upazila, Sunamganj. Shah Abdul Karim was born in Ujandhal village in neighbouring Taral Union.

According to police and local residents, Shawkat Ali, an expatriate living in the United Kingdom who hails from Hatia, had arranged a small musical gathering at his home to celebrate his daughter’s birthday. Two local female Baul singers, Tanisha and Nila, were scheduled to perform.

On Wednesday, Ataur Ali and Kamrul Hasan submitted a written application to the officer-in-charge (OC) of Dirai Police Station on behalf of villagers, objecting to the event. The police subsequently spoke to Shawkat Ali, who then cancelled the programme.

The application stated that Hatia village had long been known for its religious values and Islamic traditions. It has an Alim madrasah and a shrine dedicated to a Muslim saint, and many Islamic scholars live there.

The applicants claimed that allowing an event featuring female singers could create tension and lead to an undesirable situation in the area. They requested the authorities to take necessary measures to protect the village’s religious traditions and social harmony.

Women’s football match in Sunamganj suspended after objections from some

Kamrul Hasan, one of the complainants, said, “There used to be musical events in our village, but such programmes are no longer held. We have mosques and madrasahs, and religious gatherings are organised every year.”

“The programme featuring female singers raised concerns among villagers about possible discontent and disorder. Many believe there could be obscenity in the name of music. For this reason, they requested that the event be stopped on religious grounds,” he added.

Shawkat Ali said he had arranged a small musical event at home for his daughter’s birthday. After objections were raised and he received a phone call from the police station, he cancelled the programme, taking social harmony into consideration.

Dirai Police Station OC Aminul Islam told Prothom Alo, “I looked into the matter and found that it was a private Baul music gathering. After objections were raised, the police spoke to the organiser. He later informed us that he would not hold the musical event.”

Earlier, a friendly football match between women’s teams had to be cancelled after the Committee for Preventing Anti-Islamic Activities in Dirai objected to it.

The match was scheduled to take place at the stadium in Dirai upazila headquarters on 5 October between local club Swapnachura Sporting Club and Zara Sporting Club of Sylhet. The cancellation sparked widespread discussion and criticism.

Jahangir Alam, vice-president of the Sunamganj district committee of Udichi Shilpigoshthi, said objections had previously been raised against women’s football, and now a group’s objections had led to the cancellation of a Baul music event. He said it was regrettable that two events had been cancelled or suspended following local objections in quick succession.

He added that although the objections were framed as efforts to protect religious values and social harmony, the administration and law enforcement agencies needed to consider how cultural activities and opportunities for women to participate in sports could be safeguarded in such circumstances.
