item.title: Body of Saudi missile strike victim Shahed reaches Bogra
item.description:
The body of expatriate Bangladeshi Shahed Ahmed Ashik, 35, who was killed in a missile strike in Saudi Arabia, was taken to his home in Madla village of Shahjahanpur upazila, Bogra, around 2:30pm on Friday.
The arrival of his body triggered an outpouring of grief, with relatives breaking down in tears. Shahed, the family’s sole breadwinner, left behind his wife and two children, who now face an uncertain future.
His body is scheduled to be buried beside his grandfather’s grave in the family courtyard after the namaj-e janaza at the local high school ground at 5:00pm on Friday.
Earlier in the morning, Shahed’s wife, Kakoli Begum, and their two children went to Dhaka to receive his body. They later brought it to their village home, where relatives gathered to mourn his death.
Shahed’s brother, Masum Rana, said Shahed arrived at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh at around 5:00pm Saudi local time on October 10 and spoke to his wife over the phone.
Shortly afterwards, a missile struck the airport’s Terminal 3 area, killing Shahed along with several others, Masum said.
He said the family received Shahed’s body in Dhaka on Friday morning before bringing it to their village home. The body arrived at around 2:30pm and will be buried beside their grandfather’s grave following the namaz e janaza.
Shahed’s father, Rafiqul Islam, also lives in Saudi Arabia for work. With both of his parents abroad during the family’s time of grief, relatives said the tragedy has become even more difficult to bear.
Shahed’s sudden death has cast a pall of grief over his family and relatives. His wife and two children are now facing not only the pain of losing their loved one but also uncertainty over their future.

item.title: 20 fishermen jailed for defying ilish netting ban in Chandpur
item.description:
A mobile court has sentenced 20 fishermen to different terms of imprisonment for catching ilish in the Padma-Meghna sanctuary in Chandpur, defying a fishing ban.
Of them, 13 fishermen were given 10 days in prison each, while the remaining seven received 15 days' imprisonment each. Each fisherman was also fined Tk 1,000, bringing the total fine to Tk 20,000.
The fishermen are residents of different villages in Laxmipur Model union under Chandpur Sadar upazila.
Md Mizanur Rahman, assistant fisheries officer of Sadar upazila, told UNB that a district task force, led by Assistant Commissioner and Executive Magistrate Md. Najmul Huda, conducted the drive from 4:00pm to 9:00pm on Thursday.
During the drive, the team detained 20 fishermen and seized 30 kg of ilish, 35,000 metres of illegal monofilament fishing nets (locally known as current nets), and three engine-run fishing boats.
The seized ilish were distributed among an orphanage and needy people on Friday morning, while the boats were handed over to the Bangladesh Coast Guard for safekeeping.
The seized fishing nets were burnt in the presence of the executive magistrate.
A 22-day fishing ban in a 70-kilometre sanctuary along the Padma-Meghna rivers in Chandpur began on October 8 and will remain in force until midnight on October 29.
During the ban, catching, buying, selling, storing and transporting all types of fish, including ilish, in the designated rivers are prohibited.
District administration officials said violators will face imprisonment and fines under the law.

item.title: Tongi madrasa teacher arrested over alleged sexual assault of first-grade student
item.description:
A madrasa teacher was arrested in Tongi, Gazipur, on Thursday over allegations of sexually assaulting a first-grade student, a day after the teacher was beaten by the child’s relatives and local residents in an incident captured in videos circulating on social media.
The incident took place at a madrasa in the Auchpara area of Tongi on Wednesday. Police rescued the teacher, Moslem Ahmed, 30, and took him into custody.
He was arrested in a case filed by the child’s father and sent to court on Thursday afternoon. The madrasa authorities also filed a separate complaint alleging vandalism and assaults on teachers.
Several videos showing the teacher being beaten have been circulating on Facebook since Thursday. In a 24-second video, several people are seen questioning him inside the madrasa.
The teacher is heard saying: “...I have a different kind of relationship with our students, with everyone, especially those in first-grade. At one point, I said, kiss...” The child’s relatives then begin slapping and beating him, asking: “What kiss, huh?”
Another video, lasting 2 minutes and 29 seconds, shows several people assaulting the teacher as others attempt to intervene and pull him away. Some of the child’s relatives are also seen accusing the madrasa authorities of failing to act after being informed of the alleged incident.
According to the case statement, the alleged sexual assault took place on the stairs on the madrasa’s ground floor on Monday.
Family members and local sources said the child initially refused to return to the madrasa but did not explain why. She later disclosed the alleged incident after her parents questioned her.
The family went to the madrasa on Wednesday afternoon to question the teacher, drawing a crowd of local residents. The teacher was beaten before police arrived and took him to the police station.
The child’s father told journalists that his daughter studies in first-grade at the madrasa and that Moslem Ahmed had behaved inappropriately with her on Monday. He confirmed filing a case and said the teacher had been arrested.
Almas Hossain, the madrasa’s founder and principal, claimed the incident had been orchestrated to damage the institution’s reputation. He alleged that a group of 15 to 16 people, led by the child’s father, entered the madrasa and assaulted the teacher.
Hossain said other teachers and security personnel were also beaten when they tried to intervene. He further alleged that the group vandalized the office and looted Tk17 lakh and 5 mobile phones.
The child’s father denied the looting allegations. He also claimed that he had received death threats from various quarters following the incident, including through threatening comments on social media, and said he felt unsafe.
Tongi West police station Officer-in-Charge Arifur Rahman said a case had been filed over the alleged sexual assault and the teacher was sent to court on Thursday. He confirmed that the madrasa authorities had lodged a separate complaint over alleged vandalism and assaults on teachers.
Regarding the threats, Arifur Rahman said both sides had verbally accused each other of making threats. Police would investigate and take necessary action, he added.

item.title: Police face rising crime concerns with limited resources
item.description:
Bangladesh Police is under growing pressure to tackle violent crime and maintain law and order, with shortages of vehicles, housing and other essential resources continuing to hamper its operational capacity.
Police-recorded murder cases increased from 3,023 in 2023 to 3,786 in 2025, a rise of around 25%, according to a September 2026 research brief by the Global Development Network (GDN).
The study, which reviewed crime and public security between September 2024 and June 2026, also documented growing concerns over mob violence, sexual violence and organized extortion.
Against this backdrop, the force continues to face longstanding logistical constraints.
Although Bangladesh Police has expanded from around 117,000 personnel in 2010 to nearly 250,000, its 639 police stations average fewer than 2 vehicles each, while nearly 90% of personnel remain without accommodation in police housing facilities.
The transport shortage worsened during the July-August 2024 uprising, when 1,074 police vehicles were damaged, including 455 that were completely burned.
The government is now planning to procure 5,830 vehicles for the force at a cost of Tk 6,609 crore. The Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec) is scheduled to consider the 2 projects for approval at a meeting on October 25.
Police personnel and former senior officials say the shortages, combined with prolonged duty hours and inadequate rest, are affecting working conditions and could undermine the force's ability to deliver effective public services.
The force's responsibilities have also expanded considerably over the past 15 years. Beyond traditional policing, specialized units have been established to handle investigations, counterterrorism, tourist safety, river policing and security on the urban transport network.
These include the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI), Tourist Police, River Police, Anti-Terrorism Unit (ATU) and Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) Police.
Analysts say increasing manpower without a corresponding expansion in transport, accommodation, technology and other infrastructure could strain operational effectiveness.
On March 30, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told parliament that police patrols and law-and-order activities had been hampered because many vehicles were burned or rendered unusable during the uprising.
He said the government was taking steps to restore police capacity and replace damaged vehicles.
For officers serving in the field, the shortages are part of everyday duty.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Friday afternoon, Demra Police Station Sub-Inspector Md Jahangir Alam said officers frequently struggled to arrange transport for official duties.
“There are practically no vehicles; we have to go on duty by human hauler (leguna),” he said.
He said police personnel routinely work 12 to 16 hours a day without additional remuneration for extended duty. Food and opportunities for adequate sleep are also insufficient, he added.
The education allowance provided for officers' children is meager compared with their needs, he said.
“Most of us, from constables to SIs, are now counting the days until retirement. We are carrying on with the job only looking at the faces of our families,” he said.
Sub-Inspector Madhab, who previously served at Adabor Police Station and Hatirjheel in Dhaka, said the vehicle shortage had worsened after the July uprising destroyed many police vehicles.
Housing, however, has been a longstanding problem, he said. Police personnel must manage commuting difficulties and family responsibilities alongside demanding work schedules.
Despite the additional workload, housing support remains inadequate, he added.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Friday afternoon, Niaz Mehedi, additional deputy commissioner of the Media and Public Relations Division of Dhaka Metropolitan Police, said officers needed proper accommodation to recover from demanding shifts.
“Police housing must certainly be of good quality so that members can rest well,” he said, adding that adequate rest was closely linked to their mental health.
He also acknowledged the need for more vehicles to improve policing in the capital.
The proposed procurement is intended to address the force's transport shortage and replace aging vehicles.
According to the Planning Commission's proposal, police stations currently have 1,237 vehicles, of which 64% are more than 10 years old. The aging fleet is disrupting routine patrols, criminal investigations and emergency response services.
The procurement will be carried out under 2 projects. One proposes spending Tk 4,328.92 crore on 4,829 operational vehicles, while the other allocates Tk 2,280.14 crore for 1,001 specialized vehicles.
According to a Planning Division source, both projects are scheduled to be placed before Ecnec for approval on October 25.
Former Inspector General of Police Abdul Kaiyum said manpower had increased over the years without a corresponding expansion in housing and transport facilities.
Without access to police accommodation, personnel face additional expenses and commuting difficulties, he said, adding that these problems had persisted for a long time.
“If the government wants ethical and professional service from police, it must think about their housing facilities and vehicle shortage,” he said.
Dhaka University teacher and crime analyst Touhidul Haque said field-level police personnel carried substantial responsibilities and faced considerable risks, yet often came under the greatest scrutiny during crises and controversies.
He said the government should address shortages of housing, food and vehicles while recognizing the additional duties police personnel perform.

item.title: Dengue: 3 more die, 1,299 hospitalized in 24hrs
item.description:
Health officials on Friday said they recorded 1,299 fresh cases of dengue onslaughts killing at least three persons in the last 24 hours.
"Out of the total infected, 159 patients were hospitalized in Barisal division, 219 in Chittagong division, 274 in Dhaka division, 131 in Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) and 116 in Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) areas, 147 in Khulna division, 100 in Mymensingh division, 113 in Rajshahi division, 38 in Rangpur division and two in Sylhet division, a Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) statement said.
Since the start of the dengue onslaughts, Bangladesh this year has witnessed so far 371 deaths while the disease inflicted 119,801.
Last year, the dengue claimed 413 lives and inflicted 1,02,861 people in the country while it claimed 575 lives and inflicted 1,01,214 people in 2024.

item.title: Three killed, four injured in Faridpur road crash
item.description:
Three people were killed and four others injured in a head-on collision between an ambulance and a passenger bus on the Dhaka-Khulna Highway in Arkandi area of Madhukhali upazila in Faridpur on Friday afternoon.
The accident occurred around 2:30pm on Friday.
Shamim Reza, station officer of Madhukhali Fire Service, said the ambulance was heading towards Magura when it collided head-on with a local bus named King Fisher coming from Magura.
Three people travelling in the ambulance died on the spot, while four others were injured, he said.
Police and fire service personnel rushed to the scene after receiving the information and launched a rescue operation.
The identities of the deceased had not been confirmed at the time of filing this report.

item.title: Asian football endorses Infantino re-election as FIFA president
item.description:
The head of the Asian Football Confederation on Friday said the region supported Gianni Infantino's bid for re-election as FIFA president following fierce criticism of his aborted World Cup selloff plan.
The 56-year-old Swiss was present at a Tokyo meeting of the AFC when president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa gave his unequivocal backing.
The AFC in August had joined UEFA (Europe) and CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) in condemning Infantino over his plan to open FIFA's premium competitions such as the World Cup to private investors.
Infantino has faced calls to quit and has lost the support of many associations in his bid to be re-elected to a fourth and final term.
"I think that we reaffirm our full commitment, of course, to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as FIFA president," said Sheikh Salman, in a significant boost to Infantino's prospects.
"I think you've visited a lot of countries in Asia. I've spoken to a lot of members within this continent.
"I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well. Your support to Gianni is very clear."
Hinting at previous discord, Sheikh Salman told the AFC Extraordinary Congress and Infantino: "Gianni, yes, we had some issues we spoke about in the past.
"But let's not relate the two things together. We need to move forward... football is strongest when we work together."
Infantino, who apologised last week for the failed project, has headed FIFA since 2016 and is running for re-election in March.
The deadline for submitting candidacies is November 18.
No heavyweight candidate has put themselves forward to run against him so far, despite outspoken condemnation especially from Europe.
Many leading European national associations have withdrawn their support for Infantino over controversies including his relationship with US President Donald Trump.

item.title: Maradona death trial verdict set for December 22
item.description:
The verdict in the trial over the 2020 death of Argentine football legend Diego Maradona will be delivered on December 22, the court announced Thursday, after six months of hearings.
The trial of seven healthcare professionals accused of negligence in the star's death concluded Thursday with brief statements from Maradona's daughter and some of the defendants.
"I hope my father receives the justice he deserves...like anyone else," said Dalma Maradona, her voice breaking with emotion.
The main defendant in the case, Leopoldo Luque, Maradona's primary doctor, declared: "I am innocent."
Maradona died at age 60 from heart failure coupled with pulmonary edema.
He was found dead in his bed on November 25, 2020, at a residence in Tigre, north of Buenos Aires, rented for his convalescence, following minor neurosurgery.
His death plunged the country into mourning in the midst of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Prosecutors requested prison sentences ranging from four to twelve years for six of the seven defendants, with the heaviest sentence -- 12 years -- sought for Luque.
In closing arguments Wednesday, Luque's defense attorneys rejected the prosecution's argument that Maradona's death was foreseeable, calling their client a "scapegoat" in the case.

item.title: France to deploy 70,000 police ahead of new protests
item.description:
France will deploy some 70,000 police nationwide as it braces for new protests this weekend after some of the worst urban violence in years erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations a week ago, the government said Friday.
President Emmanuel Macron, who according to aides is postponing a visit later this month to Nigeria and Senegal amid the crisis, held a meeting of his defense council of top ministers and officials and was to meet security forces.
He was also set to host for the first time representatives of high school pupils, whose protests over conditions at their schools sparked the movement that has broadened into a nationwide show of anger against the government at the rising cost of living.
Some 70,000 security personnel will be deployed on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at a press conference in Paris, warning that calls for violence and looting were circulating on social media.
The protests have come at a critical moment for France six months ahead of elections to replace Macron, with a new poll underlining far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner and showing her position has been strengthened by the latest events.
Adding to tensions, Le Pen is at the weekend due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans, with thousands of supporters expected but local authorities fearing clashes as opponents head to the city.
Nunez was expected to visit the city Friday to “inspect the security arrangements” at the request of the prime minister’s office, it said.
At Macron’s meeting with students, “we will present our demands to him -- which remain the same: the state of school infrastructure and an overhaul of the Parcoursup (university admissions) system,” Nathanael Combary, president of Renouveau Lyceen (High School Renewal) told AFP.
Macron’s government has sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of protests last Saturday.
In a judicial response of unprecedented firmness, courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.
On Thursday, Macron called for “the utmost severity” against “acts of delinquency,” accusing “ultra-left” groups of having sought to “bring down the republic” last weekend.
On Saturday, a second round of demonstrations is expected across France.
Lyon’s city center in the southeast will be off-limits to demonstrators this weekend, while in Paris protesters will only be allowed to march a limited route between Bastille and Nation squares.
Authorities in Marseille had also banned protests but announced Friday that a union-organized demonstration would be allowed on an “exceptional basis” -- the only one authorized in the southern Bouches-du-Rhone department.
They also reversed a decision to suspend all public transport in the city on Saturday. But in the capital, leading museums including the Louvre will be closed on Saturday while the Art Basel art fair is being cut short.
Some 20% more members of the security forces will be deployed this weekend after heavy criticism of the anticipation and intelligence gathering of police last week.
“In a country governed by the rule of law, the police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder,” said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressing alarm over reports of children being severely injured by crowd-control weapons.
The violence has tarnished the image of France ahead of elections that could be a turning point in its modern history, with the government’s debt pile also troubling investors.
A new poll by Harris Interactive for M6/RTL made after the violence showed Le Pen soaring ahead on 33-35% in the first round of voting for the presidential elections.
It predicted that hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon was on course to face her in the run-off where Le Pen would emerge as an easy winner on some 70% of the vote.

item.title: Rahul Gandhi’s nephew says Delhi exhibition forced him to remove protest photos
item.description:
Raihan Vadra, the nephew of Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, has alleged that he was forced to remove several photographs documenting youth protests in Delhi from an exhibition at a government-run cultural center, hours before its opening.
Vadra, 26, the son of Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, said the management of Bikaner House asked him to remove the photographs, describing their content as “objectionable.”
“The photos were of the youth protests in Delhi,” Vadra said in a social media post. “Apparently the content is objectionable.”
He also said he was asked to remove two photographs of the Indian national flag but refused to do so.
The management of Bikaner House said it had requested the removal of photographs that were inconsistent with its exhibition policy.
The incident comes amid growing youth-led protests against the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The demonstrations, associated with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), have emerged as a challenge to the ruling administration.
CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were released from Tihar Jail on Wednesday night. They had been arrested on allegations of trespassing at Jantar Mantar after the site was denotified as a designated protest venue.
The protesters have demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
A weeks-long sit-in protest earlier this year also put pressure on the Modi government, leading to the resignation of its education minister in July amid controversy over examination paper leaks.
The removal of the photographs has raised questions about the space available for documenting and displaying politically sensitive protests at public cultural venues.

item.title: European, Mideast foreign ministers hold talks in Istanbul
item.description:
Foreign ministers from eight European and Middle Eastern countries are set to meet in Istanbul on Friday in an unprecedented format for talks on the Strait of Hormuz and crises across the Middle East.
Ministers from Britain, France and Germany -- the so-called E3 -- as well as Italy will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group comprising Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt to discuss the Palestinians, developments in Yemen and Hormuz, and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
British foreign minister Ed Miliband’s office said the talks would essentially revolve around “the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia.”
It said Miliband “will advocate for a diplomatic solution to the (Hormuz) crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms.”
He will also stress “how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilizing the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab El-Mandeb and the Suez Canal.” it added.
France confirmed the talks on “the Iranian crisis in its various ramifications,” hailing it as a first “in this format... against a backdrop of extreme instability and uncertainty in the region.”
The meeting will aim to “strengthen coordination between Europeans and Middle Eastern countries in the face of crises that we did not choose and that affect us all,” the French foreign ministry said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan is hosting the meeting, as Turkiye steps up efforts to strengthen its regional role, including through the Mecca Defense Alliance, a defense pact launched with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August.
Turkiye has said the pact is not aimed at any specific country and remains open to others, including Egypt.
Cairo has yet to decide whether to join the alliance. On Wednesday, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt would “defend Saudi territory” and would not take part in any attack on Yemen.
Intensifying attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have forced Saudi Arabia to close its main airport and postpone a major investment conference, while a maritime blockade has threatened oil exports from the world’s largest crude exporter.
Riyadh has since secured backing from its allies.
During a surprise visit on Wednesday, President Emmanuel Macron said French forces would help protect the Red Sea oil terminal of Yanbu.
Britain announced a day earlier that it would deploy fighter jets to help Saudi Arabia defend against the growing threat of Houthi attacks.
Fidan praised regional cooperation Friday, saying, “Lasting solutions cannot be imposed from outside.”
During the talks, Fidan is expected to stress that regional security requires countries in the region to “assume responsibility” and that Turkiye prioritizes cooperation mechanisms based on “regional ownership”, according to Turkish officials.
He is also expected to say that “existing disputes should not be allowed to feed one another, conflicts should not be allowed to spread to new areas, and regional tensions should not be allowed to turn into broader instability.”
Fidan is expected to call for increased international pressure on Israel over settlement expansion and what Ankara describes as “settler terrorism.”
He will also reiterate Turkiye’s support for Saudi Arabia’s security in the face of Houthi attacks and underline the need to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb.
The Black Sea is also expected to feature prominently, with Fidan highlighting Turkiye’s efforts to prevent the Russia-Ukraine war from spilling into the region.

item.title: Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
item.description:
Officials in Tehran are preparing for renewed strikes
following media reports that the United States and Israel have been examining new options for escalating their war against Iran.
The US midterm elections on November 3 and Israel’s October 27 election have injected a political factor into how both countries are approaching the conflict, which they launched in late February.
Polls show that high energy prices brought on by the Iran war are hurting Donald Trump’s Republican Party. On October 8, the president posted on social media that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, citing “productive discussions” with Tehran. The United States last launched strikes on Iran in early September.
After the elections are over, however, Trump may feel less politically constrained.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has campaigned on a platform of regime change in Iran.
Citing senior US officials the New York Times reported on Wednesday that the United States and Israel have “developed specific plans” for a “short but intensive operation” in Iran that would include targets such as nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure, and the country’s arsenal of missiles and drones.
One official told the newspaper that the goal would be to force Iran into making “diplomatic concessions” by further weakening its economy, as negotiations to end the conflict have gone nowhere. The United States has also maintained a blockade of Iranian oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz that has sapped Tehran’s oil revenues.
Other outlets have reported similar plans in recent weeks. In early October, Axios reported that the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command “to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran.”
There are currently two US aircraft carrier strike groups in the Arabian Sea, with a third expected to arrive by late November.
On October 15, Trump told the right-wing broadcaster Newsmax that he was considering a strike on Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear complex, where US officials say Iran may have moved sensitive nuclear-related material underground.
A day later, CNN reported that Trump is considering using a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb on Iranian targets. As the MOAB creates a humungous blast wave above ground, its effectiveness in targeting underground facilities such as Pickaxe would be limited.
Iranian officials say they are prepared for another attack, with a broad response that would include strikes on US bases and energy facilities in the Gulf.
Ali Asghar Shafieian, a media adviser to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, told DW that, although the United States retains a significant technological and military advantage, Tehran’s strategy is based on preserving the regime’s hold on the country rather than matching US strength.
“The United States has the upper hand in military power and technology, but Iran’s strength is in how it deals with a crisis,” Shafieian said.
Shafieian pointed to the rapid replacement of senior officials killed in previous attacks as an example of how Tehran has tried to make its political structure more resilient. Iran has also been rebuilding missile and drone capabilities that were hit during the massive wave of strikes during the first weeks of the war.
Citing Iranian officials, the Reuters news agency reported this week that Iran is “preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war,” adding that Tehran was prolonging negotiations to try to weaken Trump ahead of the midterms.
Iran has told regional governments that US military bases and critical infrastructure could become targets if neighboring countries assist another US or Israeli operation.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that participation or cooperation by regional states would result in a “decisive and proportionate response.”
“Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution,” Araghchi posted on X Wednesday. ”But, if US chooses war over diplomacy, it’ll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure.”
Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based political analyst, told DW that Iran’s preparations extend beyond missiles and drones to prioritizing internal security.
That includes confronting armed opposition groups, preparing for possible protests and developing plans to prevent external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest.
Another conflict, he said, could bring renewed internet restrictions and a stronger mobilization of government supporters in public spaces.
“In the government’s asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible,” Ghahremanpour said.
Ghahremanpour added that some factions within Iran have supported returning to a negotiated agreement. But he believes that Washington’s demands are now considered so extensive that even Iranian officials who favor compromise struggle to build domestic support for them.
“For now, we are facing a deadlock,” Ghahremanpour said. “Iranian officials do not appear optimistic about reaching an agreement.”
Talks continue to snag on Iran’s nuclear program, which US officials say must top the agenda.
Iran’s latest proposal to the United States, sent through Qatari mediators, included an offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control, in exchange for the US’s lifting its maritime blockade, releasing frozen assets and ending military actions.
Citing data from the ship tracker Kpler, the Wall Street Journal reported this week that oil flows through Hormuz are approaching prewar levels as the US military escorts tankers and shipping companies are more willing to take risks for a bigger payoff. This raises questions about whether Iran’s leverage over oil flows might be weakening.
An escalation in the confrontation would come at a moment of severe economic pressure and growing political polarization for Iranians.
A doctor in Tehran told DW that she fears what would happen should fighting resumed. Speaking with the media in Iran remains very dangerous, and she spoke under condition of anonymity.
“The economic situation has become extremely bad,” she said. “Even if you have a good income yourself, you don’t feel good living among so many people struggling with poverty,” she added.
She expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting resumes.
A woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters and said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of confrontations on the streets.
Asked about possible attacks on underground nuclear sites, she said the issue felt increasingly detached from her everyday problems.
“What do the nuclear sites have to do with us?” she said. “They are inside mountains.”
